pages.name: Two watchers
pages.text: A first fault trips nothing, so no breaker tells you it is there. Yet it leaves the healthy phases one failure from a short through the hull. So ship rules require every insulated system to watch its insulation and alarm when it runs low.[^1] Three earth lamps each join one phase to the hull. They light only while you hold their Test button. On a healthy board, each sees 254 V, so all three glow the same. Beside them, an insulation monitor's dial reads 500 kΩ.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits above the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is off.

pages.name: A solid fault on L2
pages.task: A solid fault joins L2 to the hull. What voltage does L1's lamp now see?
pages.why: Each lamp shows its phase's voltage to earth. The hull now sits at L2, as in the shifting triangle. So L1 and L3 read the line voltage, 440 V, and glow brighter. The fault short-circuits L2's lamp, so it goes out.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. A solid fault joins feeder 3's L2 to the hull. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and L2's lamp is out and the other two glow brighter. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits below the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is lit.

pages.text: With every feeder's insulation down to 120 kΩ on all three phases, the lamps stay equal at 254 V. The monitor's dial falls from 500 kΩ to 20 kΩ.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation, lowered equally on every phase by damp. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits below the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is lit.

pages.name: After a wash-down
pages.task: After a wash-down, all three earth lamps glow equally. Is the insulation healthy?
pages.answer: Not necessarily, as an equal leak on every phase leaves them equal
pages.why: Equal leaks on all three phases balance. The hull stays at the star point, and each lamp keeps 254 V. Only the monitor's reading shows the fall.

pages.name: Why DC?
pages.text: The monitor pushes a small DC voltage between the system and the hull. The capacitance must charge first, so at 5 µF a phase the dial settles five times as slowly as at 1 µF.

pages.name: A VLF test
pages.task: A VLF test set runs a cable at 0.1 Hz instead of 50 Hz. At the same voltage, how does the cable's charging current compare?
pages.why: The charging current is proportional to the frequency, and 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500. The monitor takes the same idea all the way to DC. Once charged, the capacitance passes no current at all.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits above the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is off.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. A fault joins feeder 3's L1 to the hull. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and L2's lamp is the dimmest and L3's the brightest. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits below the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is lit.

pages.name: A 150 kΩ fault
pages.task: Six feeders read 3 MΩ each, 500 kΩ together. Feeder 3 develops a 150 kΩ fault. What does the dial read?
pages.why: In parallel, 500 × 150 ÷ (500 + 150) = 115 kΩ. The total is always below the lowest single path.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. A fault joins feeder 3's L1 to the hull. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits above the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is off.

pages.name: Which alarms sound?
pages.task: The 440 V board's dial reads 28.3 kΩ. Which alarm levels sound?
pages.why: An alarm sounds when the reading falls below its level. 28.3 kΩ is below 44 kΩ and 220 kΩ, but above 22 kΩ. So the same fault alarms at one setting and not at another.

pages.task: Two boards are coupled into one system, and each still has its own monitor running. What goes wrong?
pages.answer: Each monitor reads the other as a leak, so the readings are wrong
pages.why: Each monitor joins the system to the hull through its own measuring circuit. To the other monitor, that is one more leak. Their two DC voltages also mix. So run only one monitor on a connected system.[^5]

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits above the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is off.
options: Each monitor reads the other as a leak, so the readings are wrong
Nothing, as two monitors are safer than one
The monitors' current trips the coupling breaker

pages.name: Drives with filters
pages.task: Ten drives with filters are added to the board. Now the dial takes longer to settle after every change. Why?
pages.answer: Their filters add capacitance to the hull, which the DC must charge
pages.why: Each filter is a capacitor to the hull, just like the cables' own capacitance. The monitor's DC must charge all of it before the current steadies. More capacitance means a longer wait.

pages.alt: A 440 V insulated board with bars L1, L2 and L3 feeds six feeders. Each feeder leaks to the hull through its insulation. Three earth lamps, their Test button held, join the bars to the hull, and all three earth lamps glow equally. The cables' capacitance joins the bars to the hull too. An insulation monitor sends a small DC current out through every leak and back along the hull. Its needle sits above the alarm line, and its alarm lamp is off.
options: Their filters lower the insulation resistance
Their filters add capacitance to the hull, which the DC must charge
The monitor counts each drive as a feeder to read
